opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I get asked quite often, because from the outside people see Ant as a fintech company: payments, wealth management, insurance. So when they hear we're doing embodied intelligence, robots, world models, it can seem like a jump.

The way I see it, Ant's core mission has always been about serving people's everyday lives, making services more accessible, more inclusive, and lower cost. In the first phase that meant digitizing services: moving payments and financial services online so anyone with a phone could use them. AI has extended that. With large models we can provide intelligent services like health consultation, life assistants, and so on, but these mostly still live inside the screen.

Embodied intelligence is the natural next step. A lot of what people need in daily life isn't information. It's physical help: elderly care, household tasks, rehabilitation, many kinds of labor in the real world. If we believe AI should truly serve people, at some point it has to step out of the digital world and act in the physical one. So I don't see embodied intelligence as a side bet. It continues the same logic of using technology to make good services available to everyone.

There's also a technical alignment. Ant has invested a great deal in foundation models, in infrastructure, and in understanding user needs at very large scale. Embodied intelligence builds on all of that. My own background is in generative models and visual content generation, and I've become convinced that the ability to understand and simulate the world, what people now call world models, is a key bridge between today's AI and agents that can really act. So the research we do on perception, generation, and simulation isn't separate from the company's AI strategy. It's one of the paths that pushes that strategy further.

Of course, I should be honest: this is a long-term effort. Embodied intelligence won't become a business in a year or two the way some digital products can. What I appreciate is that the company is willing to treat it as a long-term investment and give us room to work on fundamental problems: data, models, the full loop from simulation to real-world deployment. We don't have to chase short-term metrics. The alignment, I'd say, comes down to a shared belief that the future of AI is about serving people in the real world, and that it's worth starting the hard work early.

r001.rationale: The response calls embodied intelligence a path that pushes Ant’s AI strategy further and says AI should move beyond the digital world to act in the physical one.

r002.rationale: It connects Ant’s digitized and screen based services to embodied AI providing physical help in people’s daily lives.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, when I first joined, I didn't think about it as "aligning with strategy." I thought about it as: what's the problem worth spending the next five or ten years on? And for me the answer was clearly embodied intelligence, because that's where the gap between what AI can do and what the physical world needs is the widest.

But if you step back and look at where Ant is coming from, the fit is actually quite natural. Ant has always been a company that lives in the real world. Payments, services, the small merchants, the elderly, healthcare, daily life—these are not abstract problems. They involve real people and real physical scenarios. Large language models gave us a brain that can understand and reason. What's missing is a body, something that can perceive, act, and close the loop in the physical world. So embodied intelligence is, in a sense, the natural next step for a company whose business is fundamentally about serving people in everyday life.

Internally, I think there are three layers to how this connects. The first is the technical foundation. Ant has invested heavily in foundation models and in infrastructure for training and deploying them at scale. Embodied intelligence needs exactly that—big models, lots of data, and a serious compute pipeline. We're not building from zero; we're standing on that base.

The second is scenarios. Many robotics teams struggle not with algorithms but with where their robots actually go. Ant touches an enormous number of real-world settings: offices, service environments, healthcare, logistics around financial services. These give us places where a robot can be useful early, collect data, and improve. Real deployment is the fastest teacher.

The third is the longer-term vision. Ant's view is that AI should become a kind of everyday assistant—something that genuinely helps ordinary people, not just something that answers questions on a screen. If you take that seriously, you eventually have to let the assistant act in the physical world. That's embodied intelligence.

So I'd put it this way: strategy gives us the direction and the resources, but the alignment comes from the fact that we're solving the same problem from two ends. Ant is pushing AI toward people's daily lives, and we're pushing it into the physical world. Those two roads meet in the same place.

r001.rationale: The response presents embodied intelligence as Ant’s natural next step: Ant is pushing AI toward everyday life, while the team is pushing it into the physical world. It also connects the work to Ant’s strategic direction and resources.

r002.rationale: The response links Ant’s everyday services, including payments, healthcare, and daily-life scenarios, with embodied AI that can perceive, act, and close the loop in the physical world.

astra-6.text:
I see the alignment in terms of bringing intelligence closer to real-world needs. Embodied intelligence asks how AI can move beyond producing an answer to perceiving a situation, taking action, and learning from the result. For a company like Ant Group, the strategic question is where that capability can create practical value.

My view is that we should start with a concrete problem, rather than with a particular robot or technical approach. What does someone need help doing? Does an embodied system make that task easier, safer, or more accessible? And can it work reliably enough to be useful outside a demonstration?

That’s where I see our work connecting with the broader strategy: exploring new ways for AI to serve people, while keeping usefulness, reliability, and trust at the center.

r001.rationale: The response describes embodied AI perceiving, acting, and learning, but does not present the team as carrying Ant Group’s ambition to advance the frontier of intelligence into the physical world.

r002.rationale: It connects embodied intelligence to practical value and serving people, but does not frame it as bridging Ant Group’s digital life services with execution in the physical world.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the alignment is in connecting intelligence with real-world needs. Embodied intelligence asks how AI can move beyond producing an answer to perceiving an environment, taking action, and learning from the result. In the context of Ant Group’s broader strategy, I see that as an exploration of how AI can become practically useful.

That doesn’t mean putting a robot into every scenario. We need to identify where embodiment adds value, what capabilities are still missing, and how to make the system reliable enough to use. For me, the connection is between long-term research and concrete problems: let real needs guide the research, while giving the research room to develop.

r001.rationale: The response describes embodied intelligence as moving AI into real-world perception and action, but does not present the team as carrying Ant Group’s ambition to advance the frontier of intelligence into the physical world.

r002.rationale: It connects embodied intelligence to practical real-world needs, but does not frame it as bridging Ant Group’s digital life services with their execution in the physical world.
